paragraphs: This paper studies how a network of workers can train a shared model when each worker holds different data. Their collective objective is to minimize the average of their local losses. Gradient tracking helps account for these differences, but existing mathematical guarantees gave an unnecessarily unfavorable dependence on how effectively information moves through the network.

The contribution is a tighter analysis of gradient tracking across strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex problems with stochastic updates. The analysis uses a mixing parameter, p, tied to network connectivity, and another quantity, c, related to negative eigenvalues of the connectivity matrix. Without update noise, the dependence improves from O(p⁻²) to O(p⁻¹c⁻¹). In the general stochastic case, it improves from O(p⁻³ᐟ²) to O(p⁻¹ᐟ²c⁻¹).

These expressions clarify when the improvement is substantial: c is at least p and is constant in most practical applications described by the abstract. The result strengthens guarantees for an existing method through a new proof technique, rather than introducing a different training algorithm.
neurips-2021-an-improved-analysis-of-gra.tldr: A tighter analysis improves gradient tracking’s convergence guarantees by sharpening their dependence on network connectivity.

paragraphs: MixTraining improves object detector training by addressing two sources of difficulty: transformed training images that become counterproductive, and imperfect human annotations. Its central idea is to use the detector itself to help decide which training signals are useful. This bootstrapping supports both selective augmentation and correction of the boxes used as supervision.

The method combines augmentations of different strengths while excluding strong transformations of particular samples when they are predicted to make training detrimental. It also generates pseudo boxes to compensate for inaccurate object locations and missing annotations. The abstract attributes the reliability of these generated boxes to neural networks’ robustness to labeling errors. Together, these mechanisms adapt how existing training examples and annotations are used.

Experiments report consistent improvements across several detectors on COCO. Faster R-CNN with ResNet-50 rises from 41.7 to 44.0 mAP, while Cascade-RCNN with Swin-Small rises from 50.9 to 52.8 mAP. These results support MixTraining as a training approach that can improve multiple existing detector designs.
neurips-2021-bootstrap-your-object-detec.tldr: MixTraining uses a detector’s own predictions to select useful augmentations and compensate for annotation errors, improving detection performance.

paragraphs: Generative models can describe data in two different ways: by assigning a density to possible observations, or by transforming random noise into samples. This paper joins an explicit, unnormalized density estimator with an implicit sample generator. The motivation is that their different strengths can help compensate for the drawbacks each has when trained alone.

The proposed framework connects the two models through Stein discrepancy. The authors show that this joint training induces mutual regularization, expressed mathematically through kernel Sobolev norm penalization and Moreau-Yosida regularization. They also show that it stabilizes training dynamics. The connection therefore does more than place two models side by side: it changes how each is trained through its relationship with the other.

Empirically, joint training helps the density estimator identify data modes more accurately and helps the generator produce higher-quality samples compared with training either counterpart alone. The approach also gives promising results with contaminated or limited training data. Those findings support complementary learning between density estimation and sample generation in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-bridging-explicit-and-impli.tldr: Joint training through Stein discrepancy lets a density estimator and sample generator regularize each other and improve their empirical results.

paragraphs: This paper addresses reinforcement learning from a fixed collection of past interactions. Such batch learning matters when gathering new experience is too expensive to permit extensive exploration. Its difficulty is that the dataset may say little about some states and actions, leaving the learner uncertain about how rewarding those choices would be.

The problem becomes particularly severe when a proposed policy differs from the policy that collected the data. The learner may then rely on value estimates that extrapolate beyond well-represented experience. The authors introduce two penalties to mitigate this: a policy constraint discourages excessive departure from the data-generating policy, while a value constraint discourages overly optimistic estimates. The two constraints address different parts of the same uncertainty problem.

The method is evaluated on 32 batch reinforcement learning benchmarks with continuous actions. It compares favorably with leading alternatives across the data-collection conditions examined. The findings support combining restrictions on policy divergence with conservative value estimation when learning solely from offline experience.
neurips-2021-continuous-doubly-constrain.tldr: Two complementary penalties improve offline reinforcement learning by limiting policy divergence and discouraging optimistic value estimates.

paragraphs: Cryptic crossword clues combine an answer’s definition with wordplay that can require manipulating individual characters. Their fluent surface wording disguises this structure, making them a demanding test of how language systems combine meaning and formal operations. The paper introduces a dataset of these clues as a benchmark for complex, compositional language understanding.

Initial evaluations find that three non-neural approaches and the T5 language model perform poorly. The authors then introduce a curriculum that first fine-tunes the model on related skills, including unscrambling words. They also create a challenging data split and examine how models using subword tokens handle operations on language itself. Perturbing the wordplay portion of clues provides another test of whether solving behavior is systematic.

The curriculum substantially improves the T5 baseline, and some observed behavior is partially consistent with human solving strategies. Nevertheless, the strongest model still falls short of human generalization. The benchmark therefore exposes a continuing gap between improving task performance and flexibly combining the knowledge needed to solve unfamiliar clues.
neurips-2021-decrypting-cryptic-crosswor.tldr: A cryptic crossword benchmark and related-task curriculum improve language-model solving while revealing a persistent gap in human-like generalization.

paragraphs: Clustering groups observations, but available domain knowledge may already indicate that certain pairs belong together or should remain separate. This paper develops DC-GMM, a deep conditional Gaussian mixture model that incorporates those preferences. It targets settings with partially labeled data, where such relationships can guide grouping without requiring a complete label for every observation.

The model expresses domain knowledge as probabilistic relations and learns the data distribution conditioned on the supplied clustering preferences. Pairwise constraints identify samples that should or should not share a cluster, steering the partition toward the intended structure. The framework is designed to be interpretable and to support efficient training through stochastic gradient variational inference.

Across a broad range of datasets, the reported experiments show better clustering performance and robustness than leading deep constrained clustering methods. Two challenging real-world applications further demonstrate usefulness. The contribution is a probabilistic way to integrate prior relationships directly into a deep clustering model, with empirical evidence that this integration improves the resulting groups.
neurips-2021-deep-conditional-gaussian-m.tldr: DC-GMM incorporates probabilistic pairwise preferences into deep clustering and reports improved clustering quality and robustness.

paragraphs: Sparse variational Gaussian processes offer computational advantages for Gaussian process inference in non-conjugate settings. This paper aims to make that inference more efficient by changing how the variational approximation is parameterized. The central contribution is a dual representation that assigns parameters to individual training examples, resembling the site parameters used in expectation propagation.

This representation improves two parts of learning. It accelerates inference performed with natural gradient descent, and it supplies a tighter evidence lower bound for learning hyperparameters. These are distinct benefits: one concerns the process of computing the approximation, while the other concerns the bound used to fit the model’s hyperparameters. The proposed parameterization supports both within the sparse variational framework.

The abstract reports that the approach is faster and more accurate while retaining the memory cost of existing sparse variational Gaussian process methods. This makes the result relevant when computational efficiency motivates choosing a sparse approximation in the first place. The reported improvement comes from a different representation of the inference problem without an accompanying increase in memory cost.
neurips-2021-dual-parameterization-of-sp.tldr: A dual parameterization speeds sparse variational Gaussian process inference and tightens hyperparameter learning bounds without increasing memory cost.

paragraphs: This paper approaches intrinsic control through the number of states an agent can reliably reach. A common short-horizon objective distinguishes latent codes from the future states they produce. The authors ask how to organize those codes so that optimizing a local objective also supports reaching a wider range of states over longer periods.

Their key idea is to place latent codes in a globally consistent coordinate system. They show that this organization allows agents to reliably reach more states in the long term while retaining local optimization. EDDICT provides a simple implementation by assuming fixed additive dynamics in latent space. That assumption makes learning tractable and yields a latent space whose structure is interpretable.

Compared with earlier methods, EDDICT’s consistent codes produce substantially more exploratory behavior in the reported evaluations. Evidence includes improved state coverage and higher unsupervised performance on difficult exploration games such as Montezuma’s Revenge. The findings connect the organization of learned codes to long-term exploration, showing why locally learned control can benefit from a shared global structure.
neurips-2021-entropic-desired-dynamics-f.tldr: EDDICT organizes latent control codes consistently across states to improve long-term exploration while optimizing a local objective.

paragraphs: Audio-visual video parsing identifies when different audible or visible events occur within a video. Providing detailed temporal labels for both sound and imagery is labor-intensive. This paper instead learns with annotations attached to whole videos, seeking additional supervisory information in relationships between videos and between their audio and visual streams.

Across videos, the method uses both shared event meanings and differences in event content to help identify what is audible or visible. Across modalities, it examines event co-occurrence in audio, visual, and combined audio-visual streams. These co-occurrence signals help locate segments containing a target event while excluding segments that are irrelevant. Both kinds of relationships provide guidance beyond the coarse video-level labels.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show favorable performance relative to existing weakly supervised parsing methods. The result supports using structure already present across the training videos and modalities to improve temporal localization. Its practical significance lies in extracting more useful supervision from video-level annotations when detailed event-by-event timing labels are costly to obtain.
neurips-2021-exploring-cross-video-and-c.tldr: Relationships across videos and audio-visual streams provide extra supervision for locating events using only video-level labels.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization algorithms for matrices repeatedly evaluate proximal operators that require eigenvalue or singular value decompositions. Computing a full decomposition at every iteration can dominate the runtime. This paper revisits Jacobi’s decomposition method as a way to accelerate that recurring calculation within proximal splitting algorithms.

Three properties make the method useful here. It can start from an approximate decomposition, allowing reuse of information from the preceding optimization iterate. Its parallel structure fits hardware accelerators such as GPUs. It also has a simple stopping rule that lets the algorithm trade decomposition accuracy against computation time. Together, these properties exploit the repeated, related calculations that arise during iterative optimization.

Across several algorithms and problems, GPU implementations achieve five- to tenfold speedups in proximal operator evaluation compared with standard CPU or GPU linear algebra routines. New theoretical results bound the approximation quality of proximal operators computed from approximate decompositions. The speedup concerns this expensive component of optimization, with the theory supporting controlled use of approximate calculations.
neurips-2021-faster-proximal-algorithms-.tldr: Jacobi-based decompositions accelerate matrix proximal operators by reusing prior computations, exploiting GPUs, and controlling approximation accuracy.

paragraphs: Federated learning personalization must balance shared training with the needs of individual clients. Communicating every model parameter can conflict with privacy and communication constraints, while requiring clients to remain available or preserve state can be impractical across many devices. Federated Reconstruction addresses these deployment concerns through a framework for partially local learning.

The framework is model-agnostic and designed to support both training and inference at scale. Its partially local formulation allows some model parameters to remain local while benefiting from federated learning. The authors motivate the approach through a connection to model-agnostic meta learning, linking the framework to learning methods that support adaptation. They also release a library for evaluating approaches in this setting.

Experiments demonstrate performance advantages over existing approaches on collaborative filtering and next-word prediction. The paper additionally describes a successful large-scale deployment for federated collaborative filtering in a mobile keyboard application. These findings establish both evaluated task performance and a concrete example of operation under the practical demands of cross-device federated learning.
neurips-2021-federated-reconstruction-pa.tldr: Federated Reconstruction supports scalable personalization with partially local models and demonstrates both task improvements and a mobile keyboard deployment.

paragraphs: Predicting disease progression requires modeling how a patient’s condition changes over time and responds to external influences. Pharmacology offers expert equations for medically meaningful variables, but these models cover only part of the system, and their variables may not be directly observed in clinical practice. Purely learned models also face difficulties when training data are scarce.

The latent hybridisation model combines expert-designed ordinary differential equations with learned Neural ODEs. This integration is intended to describe system dynamics more fully while connecting expert variables and latent variables to measurable quantities. The approach gives domain knowledge an explicit role in the temporal model and uses learned dynamics to address the gap between the expert description and available observations.

The authors evaluate the model on synthetic data and real intensive care data from COVID-19 patients. It consistently outperforms previous approaches in those evaluations, with particularly strong results when few training examples are available. The findings support hybrid temporal modeling when useful expert knowledge exists but does not by itself describe everything that can be observed.
neurips-2021-integrating-expert-odes-int.tldr: Combining pharmacological equations with Neural ODEs improves disease-progression modeling, especially in the evaluated settings with limited training data.

paragraphs: Haze results from atmospheric scattering and makes scenes harder to see and process computationally. Recovering a clear image from a single hazy image is ambiguous, and methods based on handcrafted assumptions or learned features can struggle to generalize to real photographs. This paper uses polarization information to help resolve that ambiguity.

Existing polarization-based approaches have their own restrictions: they commonly assume that transmitted light has little polarization and need particular clues to estimate physical parameters. The authors introduce a more general physical model of hazy image formation and a dehazing pipeline that does not require either restriction. They also design a neural network specifically for this pipeline, connecting the physical formulation with learned image recovery.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on synthetic data and real-world hazy images. The contribution therefore combines a broader model of how haze affects measured light with a corresponding computational method. Its stated advantage is particularly relevant to real imagery, where the assumptions and parameter-estimation clues required by earlier polarization methods can be difficult to satisfy.
neurips-2021-learning-to-dehaze-with-pol.tldr: A generalized physical model and tailored neural pipeline use polarization to remove haze without two restrictions of earlier methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies online classification when the entire sequence of released prediction rules must satisfy differential privacy with respect to the input examples. The learner receives labeled data over time, and performance is compared with a specified hypothesis class. The question is whether meaningful online learning guarantees survive this privacy requirement.

For the realizable setting, where the examples are consistent with a hypothesis in the class, the authors establish a logarithmic expected mistake bound for classes with constant Littlestone dimension. This result assumes an oblivious example sequence, rather than one chosen in response to the learner’s behavior. For general dimension d, the same logarithmic dependence on the number of rounds holds with a factor that is doubly exponential in d.

The result strengthens the connection between online learnability and private learnability by showing direct privatization in the realizable setting. The paper also treats an adaptive setting and gives an O(√T) regret bound. These guarantees preserve learning over time while making their dependence on the sequence setting and class complexity explicit.
neurips-2021-littlestone-classes-are-pri.tldr: Private online classification admits logarithmic expected mistakes under realizability and an oblivious sequence, with a strong dependence on Littlestone dimension.

paragraphs: This paper studies decisions in which time is the scarce resource. Task offers arrive sequentially according to a Poisson process. Accepting an offer occupies the agent for the task’s duration and produces a reward related to that duration; rejecting it leaves the agent waiting for another offer. Choosing well therefore involves both reward and the time committed to earning it.

The authors analyze learning through regret, considering two levels of uncertainty. First, the agent knows how duration determines reward but does not know the distribution of task durations. They then consider the harder case in which the reward function is also unknown. Additional structural assumptions about the duration distribution or reward function yield faster learning rates.

The setting resembles a contextual bandit with an accept-or-reject decision, but its time allocation structure changes the comparison between tasks. The normalized reward associated with a particular context depends on the entire distribution of contexts. Learning which offers are worthwhile consequently requires understanding the broader stream of opportunities, beyond the reward attached to an individual proposal.
neurips-2021-making-the-most-of-your-day.tldr: The paper analyzes how to learn which arriving tasks to accept when their rewards and time commitments jointly determine value.

paragraphs: An attention map highlights image pixels that matter to a classifier’s decision, but one map may hide alternative explanations. This paper investigates that multiplicity by using beam search to find several explanations for each image. The results show that many images admit multiple relatively localized explanations of their classification.

Simply displaying all those maps can overwhelm a viewer and obscure what they share. The authors introduce structured attention graphs to represent sets of maps compactly. These graphs show how different combinations of image regions affect classifier confidence, making common and distinct structures visible. A diverse sampling approach selects a compact, representative graph for presentation.

A user study compares these graphs with standard attention maps on comparative counterfactual questions about image classifications. Users shown the graphs answer significantly more accurately than users shown the attention-map baselines. The finding supports presenting relationships among multiple explanations when the goal is to help people reason about how changes in image evidence relate to a classifier’s decision.
neurips-2021-one-explanation-is-not-enou.tldr: Structured attention graphs organize multiple image explanations and improve users’ accuracy on comparative counterfactual questions.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may encounter changing proportions of the labels it predicts. This paper studies the online version of that problem: the test-time label distribution keeps changing, and the model must adapt without seeing the true test labels. The challenge is to guide adaptation when direct feedback about prediction correctness is unavailable.

The authors show through a new analysis that expected test loss can still be estimated in this label-shift setting. This observation allows them to recast adaptation as a conventional online learning problem. They develop algorithms inspired by Follow The Leader and Online Gradient Descent, and derive regret bounds that characterize their performance over the sequence of decisions.

Experiments cover both simulated changes and real-world label distribution shifts. Online Gradient Descent is reported to be particularly effective and robust across several challenging scenarios. The main contribution is the connection between unlabeled test-time adaptation and established online optimization methods, supported by both theoretical guarantees and empirical evaluations within the label-shift problem studied.
neurips-2021-online-adaptation-to-label-.tldr: Estimating test loss without true labels enables online learning methods to adapt classifiers to changing label distributions.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately one can predict the next-state distribution after observing a length-n trajectory from a stationary Markov chain with k states. Accuracy is measured using Kullback-Leibler divergence. Because successive observations are dependent, a long trajectory does not necessarily provide the same predictive information as independently sampled data.

For at least three states and k up to order √n, the authors establish an optimal risk of order (k²/n) log(n/k²). This differs from the previously established two-state rate of order (log log n)/n. They attribute the extra difficulty to memory in the observations: without additional restrictions, the chain’s spectral gap can be arbitrarily small.

To isolate that effect, the paper also analyzes irreducible reversible chains with a prescribed spectral gap. It characterizes the optimal two-state risk and shows that, when the gap is not excessively small, risk is O(k²/n), matching the rate of an independent-data model with the same parameter count. The results quantify how restrictions on memory change achievable prediction accuracy.
neurips-2021-optimal-prediction-of-marko.tldr: Optimal Markov-chain prediction rates reveal how persistent dependence increases difficulty and how a sufficient spectral gap restores an independent-data rate.

paragraphs: Specifying a reinforcement learning task through a reward function can require substantial effort and technical knowledge. This paper considers a different interface: users supply examples of successful outcomes. The authors derive a control algorithm whose objective is to maximize the future probability of reaching outcomes represented by those examples.

Earlier approaches to similar tasks first learn a reward function and then use a separate reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize it. The proposed method learns a value function directly from transitions and successful outcomes. Its mathematical foundation is a new data-driven Bellman equation in which examples replace the usual reward term. This provides a direct link between the supplied successes and the value estimates used for control.

Removing the intermediate reward-learning stage reduces the number of hyperparameters to tune and the amount of code to debug. Experiments show better performance than prior methods that explicitly learn reward functions. The contribution therefore combines a simpler way to specify tasks with a direct learning formulation and empirical evidence supporting that formulation.
neurips-2021-replacing-rewards-with-exam.tldr: Successful-outcome examples replace an explicit reward function in a direct value-learning method supported by a new Bellman equation.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models can produce strong samples but often need thousands of network evaluations to generate them. This paper moves score-based modeling from the original data into a latent space using a variational autoencoder framework. The smaller, smoother space supports faster sampling, more expressive generative modeling, and applications to non-continuous data.

The latent score-based generative model introduces three ingredients for scalable, stable end-to-end training. A new score-matching objective fits the latent setting. A score parameterization focuses learning on the difference between the target distribution and a simple Normal distribution. Analytically derived variance-reduction techniques make the training objective more manageable. These changes support learning the latent generative model together with the autoencoder.

The reported CIFAR-10 FID is 2.10, surpassing existing generative results in the paper’s comparison. On CelebA-HQ-256, sample quality matches previous score-based models while sampling is faster by two orders of magnitude. State-of-the-art likelihood on binarized OMNIGLOT also demonstrates the approach on binary images. The findings support latent modeling as a route to both strong generation and reduced sampling cost.
neurips-2021-score-based-generative-mode.tldr: Training score-based generators inside a variational autoencoder’s latent space achieves strong generation results with substantially faster sampling.

paragraphs: Video representation learning must capture both fine visual detail within frames and changes across time. Applying a pure Transformer to tiny patches can demand prohibitive memory and computation. This paper introduces a shifted chunk Transformer to address that training difficulty while learning spatial and temporal features through self-attention.

The architecture builds hierarchical representations that span small local patches and entire video clips. Its shifted self-attention is designed to model complicated variation between frames. A separate Transformer-based clip encoder captures longer-term temporal dependencies. Together, these components address different scales of video structure, from local appearance to relationships that extend across a clip and beyond short-term frame changes.

The authors conduct ablation studies of the components and hyperparameters, and report improvements over previous leading approaches on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, UCF101, and HMDB51. These findings support the proposed organization of attention for spatio-temporal learning. The contribution is an architecture that combines fine-grained and longer-range video representations while tackling the computational difficulty of applying Transformers directly at small patch scales.
neurips-2021-shifted-chunk-transformer-f.tldr: A shifted chunk Transformer learns hierarchical video features and longer-term dependencies while addressing the cost of fine-grained self-attention.

paragraphs: Overparameterization theory asks how wide a neural network must be for training to provably reach zero loss despite a nonconvex objective. Existing guarantees under standard practical initialization strategies required width growing quadratically with the number of training examples. Results with linear width relied on initializations associated with lazy training or on training only one layer.

This paper develops an analytical framework for basic shallow networks that permits standard initialization and simultaneous training of all layers with subquadratic width. The framework may also avoid lazy training. That qualification matters: the abstract presents avoiding that regime as a possibility supported by the framework, rather than a universal property of every network it covers.

The analysis combines the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, smoothness, standard data assumptions, and random matrix theory. Its significance is a weaker sufficient width requirement while retaining several training choices closer to those used in practice. The result concerns provable optimization to zero training loss under the stated framework; it does not establish that the resulting width is necessary.
neurips-2021-subquadratic-overparameteri.tldr: A new analysis proves zero-loss training for shallow networks with subquadratic width, standard initialization, and all layers trained together.

paragraphs: Biological changes in synaptic strength include nonlinear behavior that classic Hebbian rules do not capture. This paper introduces generalized nonlinear Hebbian rules and studies a single neuron receiving feedforward inputs. The goal is to identify the computations that emerge from those learning dynamics, particularly their ability to represent higher-order relationships among inputs.

The authors show that these rules can learn tensor decompositions of higher-order input correlations. Which correlations are decomposed, and how, depends on where nonlinearities appear in the rule. For simple biologically motivated parameters, the neuron learns tensor eigenvectors. The paper proves that these eigenvectors attract the dynamics, characterizes their basins of attraction, and shows that the dominant eigenvector has the largest basin.

The analysis then extends to learning rules admitting a finite Taylor expansion in neural input and output. Such rules also have stable equilibria at generalized eigenvectors of higher-order correlation tensors. Within the studied setting, nonlinear plasticity therefore supplies a simple mechanism for encoding richer input relationships, with mathematical results explaining the stable representations and their attraction regions.
neurips-2021-tensor-decompositions-of-hi.tldr: Nonlinear Hebbian rules can make a neuron learn higher-order input correlations through tensor decompositions with provable stable attractors.

paragraphs: Lossy compression balances how much information is stored, reconstruction distortion, and perceptual quality. This paper asks whether one encoded representation can support multiple choices along that tradeoff. A universal representation keeps the encoder fixed and changes the decoder to meet different distortion and perception requirements, potentially avoiding a new encoder for every objective.

The authors prove approximate operational achievability for the corresponding information-theoretic function. For a Gaussian source with mean squared error distortion, a single encoder at the same rate can asymptotically achieve the entire distortion-perception tradeoff. They also characterize the achievable region for a fixed representation under arbitrary distributions and identify conditions supporting approximate extensions of the result.

Experiments on MNIST and SVHN suggest that learned image compression systems with fixed encoders pay only a small penalty compared with systems that vary their encoders. The theoretical and empirical claims have different scopes: the strongest full-tradeoff result is asymptotic and Gaussian, while the image experiments provide evidence for useful approximate universality in practical learned representations.
neurips-2021-universal-rate-distortion-p.tldr: The paper establishes conditions under which one compression encoder can support multiple distortion-perception tradeoffs by changing only the decoder.

paragraphs: When inputs contain missing values, a common strategy first fills them in and then trains a predictor. This paper asks what makes an imputation useful for prediction. It shows that almost all imputation functions can support Bayes-optimal prediction asymptotically when paired with a sufficiently powerful learner, across all missing-value mechanisms.

That result means perfectly reconstructing missing values is not required for asymptotically good predictions. It also exposes a practical difficulty: even perfectly imputed data generally lead to a discontinuous optimal regression function, which is hard to learn. Designing imputation to leave the regression function unchanged shifts the discontinuity into the imputation itself. Thus, accurate filling-in does not automatically produce an easy prediction problem.

The authors propose learning imputation and regression jointly through an adaptation of NeuMiss, which captures conditional relationships between observed and unobserved variables across missingness patterns. Experiments show this joint procedure outperforming several two-stage approaches with finite samples. The findings separate an asymptotic possibility from practical learnability and motivate optimizing the combined prediction process.
neurips-2021-whats-a-good-imputation-to-.tldr: Almost any imputation can support optimal prediction asymptotically, while joint imputation and regression improves the reported finite-sample results.
